# Clover

> Clover is a way of working with System, Human, and AI to produce meaningful outcomes. The system is the reality, and two actors work in it — the human and AI — running one system cycle: Context, Direction, Execution, Outcome, Growth. It sits on top of the systems an organization already runs — nothing to install, nothing to migrate onto.

Clover is a framework for reasoning about and governing AI-enabled work. It is not a mandatory process. The system is the reality, and the **actors** in it are the human and AI. The human establishes purpose, Direction, and accountability; AI provides capability and determines how work happens within human Direction. The **system cycle** those actors run is **Context → Direction → Execution → Outcome → Growth**.

Clover is not a new way of working. Every system that worked in the past has worked this way: somebody understood the situation, somebody decided what mattered and answered for it, the work got done, reality showed what happened, and what it taught carried into the next attempt. AI does not change that cycle. It makes every stage easier, better and faster: Context is easier to build with the human and AI helping each other understand the system, Direction is easier to identify and to pursue, Execution is faster and better because the Context and Direction behind it are better, and Outcomes are easier to validate against the real system without tampering. Every stage feeds the learning and the growth of the system, and all the actors grow with it. What AI did change is that execution moved to something that cannot be accountable, and accountability went out of scope with it. A model can perform the work, report that it worked, and hold nothing when it did not. Clover establishes accountability back into the system, through the human actor who can truly take up the role. AI takes its place as an actor inside the existing cycle rather than as a replacement for it. AI capability may scale, but accountability cannot; AI cannot carry it, and it can make it visible.

The five stages of the system cycle. Context is the relevant evidence about system reality needed for the current work. Direction is the human-defined outcome, priorities, constraints, boundaries, and accountability. Execution is AI determining and executing the path within that Context and Direction. Outcome is what the real system or environment shows actually happened, favorable or not. Growth is whatever that Outcome taught, carried back into Context.

What makes Clover distinct is the relationship between those five stages and the authority boundary around them. The claim is testable: context should become more inspectable, Direction more explicit, execution safely delegable where evidence supports it, and Outcome harder to claim without environmental evidence tied to the intended outcome. A team should keep Clover only where applying it improves observable work.

**Capability may scale. Direction remains human.** Competitive pressure or stronger models may increase delegated execution inside Execution. They do not transfer purpose, acceptable risk, priorities, boundaries, or accountability to AI.

Clover's boundaries sit inside the law, never above it. Legal, regulatory and organizational obligations are set outside Clover, and where one of them disagrees with a Clover boundary, the obligation wins. Clover is a way of working, and adopting it certifies nothing. A boundary comes from human Direction and can be widened or narrowed by the accountable human. An obligation cannot be traded away by anyone inside a cycle. What Clover does is keep the cycle arranged so those obligations stay satisfiable: the System able to show what happened, the Human reachable and able to intervene, the AI disclosed.

Delegated execution is an engineering decision. Consider evidence from comparable outcomes, blast radius, observability, reversibility, and approval boundaries. **Delegation can move work. It does not move Direction.**

A failed result returns the cycle to Context with new information. The goal is not to retry the same Execution on the same evidence.

When a boundary matters to Outcome, an implementation should prefer runtime enforcement over model instructions alone. Verification controls can be protected outside the model with filesystem permissions, containers, CI identities, protected branches, tool gateways, MCP policies, or equivalent environment controls. Clover does not require a particular implementation, and the framework does not claim that its current orchestration engine automatically enforces every such control.

Growth is the fifth stage of the system cycle: whatever the Outcome taught, at any size, carried back into Context. It needs no repetition and no scale, and it is not reserved for frontier AI providers learning from volumes of interaction data. One wrong answer, understood and recorded, is Growth. Growth can accumulate across humans, AI systems, the system being worked on, teams, organizations, and frontier AI development; these layers are controlled differently. Clover does not assume customer work trains an AI provider's underlying model.

Accountability follows the same scale boundary. Within a task or piece of work, the named human is accountable for the outcome they direct. This does not transfer model-level accountability onto that person. The company that builds and releases an AI model remains accountable for the model and the consequences of the controls it owns; governments and regulators enforce the duties it does not uphold voluntarily.

## Pages

- [The framework](https://cloverframework.com/): the full argument, the actors, the system cycle, and the closing claim that responsibility for AI was sidelined.
- [Getting started](https://cloverframework.com/start/): read-only system access, AGENTS.md, and a first cycle.
- [Governance](https://cloverframework.com/governance/): access, attribution, approvals, agent behavior, delegated execution, and the named human who is accountable.
- [Evidence](https://cloverframework.com/evidence/): case studies and reference implementations, each stating where it stopped.
- [Glossary](https://cloverframework.com/glossary/): plain-language definitions.
- [The author](https://cloverframework.com/author/): who wrote it.

## Core

- [AGENTS.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/AGENTS.md): Instructions for agents — stages, evidence rules, authority boundaries, failure checks, and context handoff.
- [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/README.md): What Clover is, what makes it distinct, the five stages, adoption, and limits.
- [The five stages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/04-framework.md): The framework, distinction, delegated execution, and evaluation model.
- [Principles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/03-principles.md): One principle per stage, including the human Direction boundary.

## Putting it into practice

- [The orchestration environment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/orchestration-environment.md): The access layer that feeds Context — what to connect, how to grant access safely, and a build sequence ordered by increasing risk.
- [Context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/05-context-engineering.md): Why context matters and where persistent context files should live.
- [Adoption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/09-adoption.md): How to test whether Clover changes observable work.
- [Governance](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/08-governance.md): Ownership, approval, attribution, access, and delegated execution.
- [Outcome in practice](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/07-outcome.md): What counts as evidence of the intended outcome.
- [Quickstart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/QUICKSTART.md): First cycle in about 15 minutes.
- [Orchestration brief template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/templates/orchestration-brief.md): One-page working artifact covering every stage.

## Evidence

- [Why Responsibility for AI Was Sidelined](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/ai-responsibility/why-responsibility-was-sidelined.md): the master claim, direct sources, evidence limits, and links to the supporting papers.
- [Reference implementations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/reference-implementations.md): Patterns for system access, AI-enabled work, and runtime enforcement boundaries.
- [Runtime enforcement reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/reference/runtime-enforcement/): Executable examples showing how verification boundaries can be enforced outside the model.
- [Case studies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/case-studies/README.md): Delivered outcomes, each stating what it has not shown.
- [How AI fails](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/how-ai-fails.md): Failure modes and the stage that catches each.
- [Practices and field lessons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/santhoshsathish94/clover-framework/main/docs/field-practices.md): Lessons from real work, including failures.
